lectures.title: Parliament: Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha - composition and members

items: **Parliament** consists of President + Lok Sabha + Rajya Sabha (the President is an integral part, not a member of either House).
Duration of Houses; Art. 83(1): duration of Rajya Sabha (permanent House)
Speaker & Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha
Allocation of seats in Rajya Sabha
Indian Polity #2; Indian Polity #12; Indian Polity #13

**Maximum strength:** 550: not more than 530 members from the States (directly elected) and not more than 20 members from the Union Territories. It was 552 while 2 Anglo-Indian members could be nominated.

**Anglo-Indian members:** the earlier provision for 2 nominated Anglo-Indian members under Art. 331 has been discontinued by the 104th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2019; abolished after 25 January 2020. Nominated Anglo-Indian members no longer exist.
**Present strength:** 543 elected members (524 from States + 19 from UTs).
**A person must be:** 1. A citizen of India.
**Age:** 2. Not less than 25 years of age (minimum age 25 years).
**Voter:** 3. Registered as a voter in any parliamentary constituency.
**Office of profit:** 4. Not hold any office of profit.
**Others:** 5. Not of unsound mind, undischarged insolvent, etc. (as per Representation of the People Act).
**Art. 102:** disqualification under Art. 102 and the Representation of the People Act, 1951.
**Tenth Schedule (Anti-Defection Law):** decided by the Speaker.
**Member of both Houses:** if he becomes a member of both Houses, he must choose one within 10 days.
**Two constituencies:** a person can contest from maximum two constituencies.

parts.t: Lok Sabha: term, vacation of seats and reservation
items: **Normal term:** 5 years from the date of first sitting (Art. 83).
**Dissolution:** can be dissolved earlier by the President.
**National Emergency:** during National Emergency the term can be extended by Parliament for 1 year at a time.
Becoming a member of the other House
**SC/ST:** seats reserved for Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes in proportion to their population.
**Duration:** reservation was initially for 10 years; repeatedly extended (last extended by 104th Amendment till 2030).
**Non-member Minister:** a Minister who is not a member of Lok Sabha/Rajya Sabha must get elected within 6 months.
**Council of Ministers:** strength limited to 15% of total membership of Lok Sabha (91st Amendment).
**Maximum strength:** 250: not more than 238 representatives of the States and Union Territories (elected) and 12 members nominated by the President.
**Union Territories:** only 3 Union Territories have representation: Delhi, Puducherry and Jammu & Kashmir.
**Mode of election:** indirect election by the elected members of the State Legislative Assemblies.
**System:** Proportional Representation by means of Single Transferable Vote.
**Allocation of seats:** allocation among States is based on population (Fourth Schedule).
**Nominated members:** persons having special knowledge or practical experience in Literature, Science, Art and Social Service.
**A person must be:** 1. A citizen of India.
**Age:** 2. Not less than 30 years of age.
**Voter:** 3. Registered as a voter in any parliamentary constituency.
**Office of profit:** 4. Not hold any office of profit.
**Disqualifications:** 5. Other disqualifications same as Lok Sabha (Art. 102 + RPA, 1951 + Tenth Schedule).
**Retirement:** as nearly as possible, one-third of members retire every two years.
**Casual vacancy:** filled for the remainder of the term.
**Decision on Anti-Defection:** Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
**1. Art. 249:** can authorise Parliament to legislate on a State List subject in national interest (2/3rd majority of members present & voting).
**2. Art. 312:** can initiate creation of new All-India Services (2/3rd majority).
**3. Constitutional Amendment Bills:** equal powers with Lok Sabha.
**4. Introduction of Bills:** can introduce Ordinary Bills and Constitutional Amendment Bills.

parts.t: Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha compared
items: 550 (552 with the 2 Anglo-Indian nominees, now discontinued)
**First General Election to Lok Sabha:** 1951-52 (first session of 1st Lok Sabha: 13 May 1952).
**First Speaker of Lok Sabha:** G.V. Mavalankar. The first Indian Speaker of the Central Legislative Assembly, elected in 1925, was Vithalbhai J. Patel.
**First Tribal Speaker of Lok Sabha:** P.A. Sangma (1996).
**First no-confidence motion:** moved by Acharya J.B. Kripalani against Nehru's government (3rd Lok Sabha, 1963).
**First joint sitting of Parliament:** 1961 (Dowry Prohibition Bill).
**First actress nominated to Rajya Sabha:** Nargis Dutt (1980).
**Leader of Opposition:** first recognised in Lok Sabha in 1969.
Set up first in 1921 (under GoI Act 1919)
Constituted for the first time in 1950
Constituted 1997; first such committee by any Indian legislature

lectures.title: Bills in Parliament: types, procedure and joint sitting

items: **Bill:** proposed legislation; becomes an Act only after President's assent under Art. 111.
**Ordinary Bill:** introduced in either House; both Houses hold equal legislative powers.
**Money Bill:** introduced only in Lok Sabha with prior recommendation of President; Rajya Sabha has recommendatory role only.
**Constitution Amendment Bill:** introduced in either House; passed separately by each House by special majority; No Joint Sitting.
**Rule:** "Every Money Bill is a Financial Bill, but every Financial Bill is NOT a Money Bill."
**Introduction:** introduced in either House (Lok Sabha / Rajya Sabha).
**Passing:** passed by simple majority; joint sitting (Art. 108) possible in case of deadlock.
**Rajya Sabha:** has no fixed constitutional time limit to consider it.
**Introduction:** introduced only in Lok Sabha with prior recommendation of President.
**Rajya Sabha:** can only make recommendations within 14 days (cannot amend or reject).
**Speaker:** Lok Sabha Speaker's decision under Art. 110(3) is final; No Joint Sitting.
**Contents:** includes taxes, borrowings, custody of/withdrawal from Consolidated Fund; does not include mere fines/penalties.
**Contents:** contains matters of Art. 110 + general legislation.
**Introduction:** introduced only in Lok Sabha on President's recommendation.
**Rajya Sabha:** has full power to reject/amend; Joint Sitting is possible.
**Contents:** involves expenditure from Consolidated Fund of India without Art. 110 matters.
**Introduction:** introduced in either House; President's recommendation needed before consideration; Joint Sitting is possible.
**Private Member's Bill:** introduced by any MP who is not a Minister (does not mean nominated member).

parts.t: Ordinary, Money and Constitution Amendment Bills compared
items: Either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha
Either Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha
**Readings:** general discussion on a Bill takes place during the Second Reading (not First or Third).
**Joint Sitting (Art. 108):** summoned by President (expresses intention); presided over by Lok Sabha Speaker (if absent: Deputy Speaker, then Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha).
**Quorum and decision:** quorum is 1/10th; decides by simple majority.
Dowry Prohibition Bill (first joint sitting of Parliament)
**3 Joint Sittings** held so far: Dowry Prohibition Bill (1961), Banking Service Commission Repeal Bill (1978), POTA (2002).

lectures.title: Lok Sabha procedure: Question Hour, Zero Hour, motions and rules

parts.t: Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business
items: **Framework:** the Constitution provides the broad institutional framework; day-to-day proceedings in Lok Sabha are governed by the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha.

**Crucial exam distinction:** several major parliamentary tools (e.g., No-Confidence Motion, Zero Hour, Rule 377) are NOT mentioned in the Constitution; they derive from Rules or procedural conventions.
**Core mandate:** primary parliamentary instruments to enforce executive accountability and exercise control over the Council of Ministers.
**Primary mechanisms for executive accountability:** Question Hour, Supplementary Questions, and Adjournment Motions.
**Parliamentary Accountability Triangle:** Question Hour + Supplementary Questions + Adjournment Motions directly ensure cabinet responsibility to the legislature.
**Question Hour:** first hour of every parliamentary sitting dedicated to asking and answering questions.
**Timings:** Lok Sabha: 11:00 AM - 12:00 Noon; Rajya Sabha: 12:00 Noon - 1:00 PM (shifted after 2014).
First hour of every sitting (11 AM-12 Noon)
Immediately follows Question Hour (12 Noon-1 PM)
Provided under Rules of Procedure; formally codified
Informal convention (Not in Constitution or Rules); duration not fixed in Rules
Asking and answering classified questions; questioning Ministers on administrative actions
Raising urgent matters of great public importance without prior notice
**Zero Hour** is NOT a constitutional provision.
Requires an oral answer on the floor of the House; maximum 20 starred questions listed for oral answer per day
Requires a written answer laid on the table
Urgent matter of public importance; asked with notice shorter than 10 clear days (the standard prescribed period); receives an oral answer
**Starred vs Unstarred trap:** Starred - Oral + Supplementary Questions permitted; Unstarred - Written + NO Supplementary Questions.
**No-Confidence Motion (Rule 198):** not mentioned in the Constitution; introduced ONLY in Lok Sabha (can NOT be moved in Rajya Sabha).
**Against whom:** moved against the entire Council of Ministers (cannot be moved against an individual minister).
**Notice and support:** requires written notice to the Secretary-General and the support of at least 50 members for leave to be granted.
**Confidence Motion:** moved by the Council of Ministers/Government to demonstrate majority support on the floor.
**First no-confidence motion:** moved by Acharya J.B. Kripalani against Nehru's government (3rd Lok Sabha, 1963).
**Rule 184 (Discussion + Voting):** substantive motion; permits discussion on a specific matter of public interest followed by voting (carries significant political consequences for the government).

**Rule 377 (Special Mention of Matters):** allows members to raise matters of general public importance that cannot be raised under rules governing Questions, Calling Attention, or other formal Motions.
**Rule 377 conditions:** requires written notice and Speaker's consent; 20 matters may be raised on a day.
**Rule 8(1):** governs the procedure for the election of the Deputy Speaker (date fixed by the Speaker and notified by the Secretary-General).
Substantive motion requiring discussion with voting
**Adjournment Motion:** interrupts normal business to discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance and recent occurrence; involves an element of censure/condemnation against the government.
**Adjournment Motion requirements:** must relate to a single, definite, specific matter of recent occurrence; cannot raise a question of privilege; only one Adjournment Motion allowed per sitting.
**Calling Attention Motion:** Indian parliamentary innovation to draw the attention of a Minister to an urgent matter of public importance.
**No censure:** Calling Attention resembles an Adjournment Motion but does NOT contain (carry) an element of censure/condemnation against the government.
Call attention of a Minister to an urgent public matter
Discuss a definite matter of urgent public importance
Does not disrupt the scheduled daily agenda
Interrupts and suspends normal parliamentary business
Restricted the scope of Adjournment Motion
Admissible only when other tools (e.g., Short Duration) are too late
**Scope restriction:** Calling Attention notices historically restricted the operational scope of Adjournment Motions (NOT Question Hour or Zero Hour).
**Indian innovations:** both Zero Hour and Calling Attention Motion are indigenous Indian contributions to parliamentary procedure.
**Closure Motion:** moved to cut short debate and put the question to vote.
**Guillotine:** a form of closure applied when allotted time expires; all remaining discussed and undiscussed clauses/demands are immediately put to vote.
